# Policy design

The fifteen reforms fall into four families: direct changes to benefit
taxation, senior-deduction and credit redesigns, employer-payroll-tax swaps, and
a reverse-Roth restructuring. We score them all against one current-law
baseline.

## Direct taxability changes

- **`option1`**: full repeal of Social Security benefit taxation beginning in
  `2026`.
- **`option2`**: tax 85 percent of all Social Security benefits by eliminating
  the current-law thresholds and applying the top statutory inclusion rate to
  all recipients.
- **`option8`**: tax 100 percent of benefits.
- **`option9`**: tax 90 percent of benefits.
- **`option10`**: tax 95 percent of benefits.
- **`tax93`**: tax 93 percent of benefits. The Social Security actuaries
  estimate that taxing the employer-funded and earnings portions of benefits in
  full would tax about 93 percent of benefits.
- **`magi100`**: count the full benefit, rather than half, in the combined
  income that the taxability thresholds test. The thresholds, inclusion rates,
  and 85 percent cap stay at current law, so beneficiaries owe tax on benefits
  at lower levels of other income and on a larger share of benefits at a given
  income.
- **`tax_panel_2005`**: the simple deduction that the President's Advisory Panel
  on Federal Tax Reform recommended [@taxpanel2005]. Taxable benefits equal half
  of income above `$22,000` (`$44,000` for joint filers), where income counts 85
  percent of benefits, up to a cap of 85 percent of benefits. At CRFB's request,
  we leave the thresholds unindexed, so they stay fixed in nominal dollars
  through `2100`.

## Senior-deduction and credit redesigns

- **`option3`**: `option2` plus permanent extension of the temporary bonus
  senior deduction.
- **`option4`**: `option2`, repeal of the bonus senior deduction, and a `$500`
  nonrefundable credit tied to Social Security tax liability.
- **`option7`**: eliminate the bonus senior deduction without otherwise
  changing the Social Security taxability structure.
- **`option11`**: `option2`, repeal of the bonus senior deduction, and a `$700`
  nonrefundable Social Security credit with a `6%` phase-out above `$150,000`
  for joint filers and `$75,000` for other filers.

Because the bonus senior deduction expires after `2028`, these reforms change a
different current law from `2029` on. A deduction's value also rises with the filer's
marginal tax rate, while a flat credit's value does not. We hold the `option11`
phase-out thresholds fixed in nominal dollars, as CRFB specified, while wages
and the other federal income-tax thresholds grow. In the late decades the credit
reduces almost no income tax, and the `option11` revenue effect converges to the
`option2` effect by `2075`.

## Employer-payroll-tax swaps

- **`option5`**: eliminate Social Security benefit taxation and instead treat
  employer payroll-tax contributions as taxable compensation.
- **`option12`**: a phased Roth-style swap that taxes employer payroll
  contributions immediately but phases out the OASDI share of benefit taxation
  first and the HI share later.

These reforms change the tax base itself and shift income tax from retirees
toward workers. We credit the income tax on employer contributions to the OASDI
and HI trust funds by the rules in @sec-swap-accounting.

We also score `option6`, a shorter phase-in variant, as a sensitivity case. It
phases the taxable share of employer contributions in from 13 percent in `2026`
to 100 percent in `2033` and phases benefit taxation out over `2029`-`2044`. The
dashboard offers `option12` as the phased Roth option and leaves `option6` off
its menu.

## Reverse-Roth proposal

- **`reverse_roth`**: tax 100 percent of Social Security benefits while
  allowing an above-the-line deduction for the employee share of Social
  Security payroll taxes paid during working years.

The reverse-Roth reform inverts the timing of Social Security's tax treatment.
Under current law, Social Security works much like a partial Roth account.
Workers cannot deduct their share of payroll tax, so they pay it from after-tax
wages, and beneficiaries later pay income tax on only part of each benefit. The
reverse-Roth design moves toward a traditional account: workers deduct their
payroll contribution when they pay it and pay income tax on the full benefit
when they receive it. The deduction goes to workers and the added tax falls on
beneficiaries, so the net revenue effect in each year depends on the relative
size of the working-age and retired populations.
